title: Σιμοείσιος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The fighting is now general, and the poem goes from kill to kill. Antilochus is the first to kill a Trojan, Echepolus; Elephenor, leader of the Abantes, is dragging the body away to strip it when Agenor spears him in the side. Ajax kills the young Simoeisius, named for the river beside which he was born, and he falls like a poplar felled for a chariot wheel. Antiphus throws at Ajax and kills Leucus, a companion of Odysseus instead; Odysseus, angry, kills Priam’s illegitimate son Democoön with a spear through the head, and the Trojans give way. Apollo calls them back from Pergamus, saying that the Achaeans are not made of stone and that Achilles is not fighting, and Athena rouses the Achaeans. The Thracian Peirous strikes down the Epean leader Diores with a rock and stabs him, and is killed in turn by Thoas of Aetolia, who cannot strip the body for the Thracian spears. The poet closes by saying that not even a man led through the midst by Athena could find fault with that day’s work.

sentences.t:
πρῶτος δ’ Ἀντίλοχος Τρώων ἕλεν ἄνδρα κορυστὴν
ἐσθλὸν ἐνὶ προμάχοισι Θαλυσιάδην Ἐχέπωλον·
sentences.tr:
prōtos d’ Antilochos Trōōn helen andra korystēn
esthlon eni promachoisi Thalysiadēn Echepōlon·
sentences.l:
And first Antilochus took a man of the Trojans, a helmeted warrior,
good among the front-fighters, Thalysius’-son Echepolus;
sentences.i: Antilochus was the first to kill a Trojan: a helmeted warrior, a good man among the foremost fighters, Echepolus, son of Thalysius;
sentences.n: ἕλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, here ‘kill’, and it has no augment (Attic εἷλεν); Τρώων ‘of the Trojans’ goes with ἄνδρα, ‘a man of the Trojans’ (not with Antilochus, who is an Achaean; the Greek puts the two words side by side, and l moves Τρώων next to ἄνδρα), and πρῶτος ‘first’ goes with Antilochus. κορυστής is built on κόρυς ‘helmet’ (the verb κορύσσω is ‘arm’), and is taken here as ‘helmeted warrior’; ‘armed’ would be the other reading. ἐσθλόν ‘good’ is the word for a man good in battle, and ἐνὶ προμάχοισι is ‘among the front-fighters’, the πρόμαχοι who fight in front of the main body (ἐνί is ἐν, and -οισι the epic dative plural). Θαλυσιάδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Thalysius’, and Ἐχέπωλον the name in apposition.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἔβαλε πρῶτος κόρυθος φάλον ἱπποδασείης,
ἐν δὲ μετώπῳ πῆξε, πέρησε δ’ ἄρ’ ὀστέον εἴσω
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη· τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν,
ἤριπε δ’ ὡς ὅτε πύργος ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ.
sentences.tr:
ton rh’ ebale prōtos korythos phalon hippodaseiēs,
en de metōpōi pēxe, perēse d’ ar’ osteon eisō
aichmē chalkeiē· ton de skotos osse kalypsen,
ēripe d’ hōs hote pyrgos eni kraterēi hysminēi.
sentences.l:
him he hit first on the ridge of the horse-haired helmet,
and in the forehead fixed it, and pierced the bone, inside,
the bronze point; and darkness covered his two eyes,
and he crashed down, as when a tower falls in strong battle.
sentences.i: He hit him first on the ridge of his helmet, thick with horsehair, and fixed the spear in his forehead, and the bronze point pierced the bone and went inside; and darkness covered his eyes, and he crashed down like a tower in strong battle.
sentences.n: τόν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘him’, and ῥ’ is the particle ῥα. κόρυθος φάλον is ‘the ridge of the helmet’ (the usual explanation of φάλος, not certain), and ἱπποδασείης, genitive agreeing with κόρυθος, is ‘thick with horsehair’. The subject of ἔβαλε and πῆξε is Antilochus (the spear is understood), but the subject of πέρησε, ‘pierced’, is αἰχμή ‘point’, which comes only in line 461. τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν is the stock phrase for death, ‘darkness covered his eyes’: τόν ‘him’ and ὄσσε (dual, ‘the two eyes’) are both accusative, the whole and its part; the same line comes at 503 and 526. ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘crash down’, and ὡς ὅτε πύργος leaves out the verb: ‘as when a tower (falls)’. ὑσμίνη is ‘battle’, here ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ ‘in strong battle’, a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ πεσόντα ποδῶν ἔλαβε κρείων Ἐλεφήνωρ
Χαλκωδοντιάδης μεγαθύμων ἀρχὸς Ἀβάντων,
ἕλκε δ’ ὑπ’ ἐκ βελέων, λελιημένος ὄφρα τάχιστα
τεύχεα συλήσειε·
sentences.tr:
ton de pesonta podōn elabe kreiōn Elephēnōr
Chalkōdontiadēs megathymōn archos Abantōn,
helke d’ hyp’ ek beleōn, leliēmenos ophra tachista
teuchea sylēseie·
sentences.l:
And him, fallen, by the feet took hold of lord Elephenor,
Chalcodon’s son, commander of the great-hearted Abantes,
and was dragging him from out under the shafts, eager that as quickly as possible
he might strip his armour;
sentences.i: Lord Elephenor, the son of Chalcodon, commander of the great-hearted Abantes, took hold of the fallen man by the feet and was dragging him out from under the shafts, eager to strip his armour as quickly as he could;
sentences.n: λαμβάνω takes the genitive of the part held, so ποδῶν ἔλαβε is ‘took hold of him by the feet’, and τὸν δὲ πεσόντα is ‘him, having fallen’ (aorist participle of πίπτω). κρείων ‘lord’ is Elephenor’s title; the next line gives his patronymic Χαλκωδοντιάδης ‘son of Chalcodon’ and his post as ἀρχός ‘commander’ of the Abantes. Line 464 is the same line as 2.541, in the Catalogue of Ships, and its English is kept. ἕλκε is an imperfect without augment (εἷλκε), ‘was dragging’, and ὑπ’ ἐκ is two prepositions together, ‘from out under’, with βελέων ‘shafts’ (the missiles in the air). λελιημένος is the perfect middle participle of λιλαίομαι, ‘eager’; ὄφρα with the optative συλήσειε (aorist of συλάω ‘strip’) gives purpose, ‘so that he might strip’, and τεύχεα is ‘armour’.

sentences.t: μίνυνθα δέ οἱ γένεθ’ ὁρμή.
sentences.tr: minyntha de hoi geneth’ hormē.
sentences.l: but briefly for him came to be his drive.
sentences.i: but his drive lasted only a little while.
sentences.n: μίνυνθα is an adverb, ‘for a short time’. γένεθ’ is ἐγένετο without its augment and with the ending elided, ‘came to be’; οἱ is the dative ‘for him’, not the article. ὁρμή is his impulse or effort, here the push to strip the corpse, and the line says it did not last.

sentences.t:
νεκρὸν γὰρ ἐρύοντα ἰδὼν μεγάθυμος Ἀγήνωρ
πλευρά, τά οἱ κύψαντι παρ’ ἀσπίδος ἐξεφαάνθη,
οὔτησε ξυστῷ χαλκήρεϊ, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.tr:
nekron gar eryonta idōn megathymos Agēnōr
pleura, ta hoi kypsanti par’ aspidos exephaanthē,
outēse xystōi chalkēreï, lyse de guia.
sentences.l:
For seeing him dragging the corpse, great-hearted Agenor
in the ribs, which for him, stooping, beside the shield were laid bare,
wounded him with a polished, bronze-fitted spear, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.i: For great-hearted Agenor, seeing him dragging the corpse, stabbed him with his polished, bronze-fitted spear in the ribs, which were laid bare beside the shield as he stooped, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.n: νεκρὸν γὰρ ἐρύοντα ἰδών: ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω ‘seeing’, and ἐρύοντα (present participle of ἐρύω ‘drag’, accusative) agrees with Elephenor, who is not named in this sentence; μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet of Agenor. πλευρά ‘ribs’ is the accusative of the part struck by οὔτησε (the man wounded, Elephenor, is understood), and τά οἱ κύψαντι παρ’ ἀσπίδος ἐξεφαάνθη is a relative clause, ‘which were laid bare for him, stooping, beside the shield’: κύψαντι is the aorist participle of κύπτω ‘bend over’ (dative, with οἱ ‘for him’), and ἐξεφαάνθη, the aorist passive of ἐκφαίνω, is singular because a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb. οὔτησε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’, a thrust at close quarters; ξυστῷ (dative) is a spear, from ξύω ‘scrape, smooth’, and its exact sense is not certain, and χαλκήρεϊ is ‘bronze-fitted’. λῦσε δὲ γυῖα ‘loosed his limbs’ is the Homeric phrase for killing.

sentences.t:
ὣς τὸν μὲν λίπε θυμός, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ δ’ ἔργον ἐτύχθη
ἀργαλέον Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ton men lipe thymos, ep’ autōi d’ ergon etychthē
argaleon Trōōn kai Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
So him left life, and over him a work was wrought
grievous, of Trojans and Achaeans;
sentences.i: So life left him, and over him a grievous work of Trojans and Achaeans was wrought;
sentences.n: λίπε is an aorist without augment (ἔλιπε), and θυμός is the life when it leaves a body, so ‘life left him’; τὸν μέν ‘him, for his part’ is Elephenor. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘over him’, over the corpse. ἔργον ἐτύχθη is ‘a work was made’ (aorist passive of τεύχω), and ‘work’ is the work of war, so ἔργον ἀργαλέον ‘grievous work’ means a hard struggle, with Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ‘of Trojans and Achaeans’ giving whose work it is.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ λύκοι ὣς
ἀλλήλοις ἐπόρουσαν, ἀνὴρ δ’ ἄνδρ’ ἐδνοπάλιζεν.
sentences.tr:
hoi de lykoi hōs
allēlois eporousan, anēr d’ andr’ ednopalizen.
sentences.l:
and they, like wolves,
rushed upon one another, and man tossed about man.
sentences.i: and like wolves they rushed upon one another, man tossing man about.
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ λύκοι ὣς is ‘and they, like wolves’: οἵ is the article used as a pronoun, and ὣς ‘like’ stands after its noun. ἐπόρουσαν is an aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush upon’, and ἀλλήλοις is the dative ‘upon one another’. ἀνὴρ δ’ ἄνδρ’ ἐδνοπάλιζεν has ἀνήρ in the nominative and ἄνδρα (elided) in the accusative, ‘man (tossed) man’; ἐδνοπάλιζεν is an imperfect of δνοπαλίζω, a rare word whose exact sense is not certain, and ‘toss about’ is the usual explanation.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἔβαλ’ Ἀνθεμίωνος υἱὸν Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
ἠΐθεον θαλερὸν Σιμοείσιον, ὅν ποτε μήτηρ
Ἴδηθεν κατιοῦσα παρ’ ὄχθῃσιν Σιμόεντος
γείνατ’, ἐπεί ῥα τοκεῦσιν ἅμ’ ἕσπετο μῆλα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
enth’ ebal’ Anthemiōnos huion Telamōnios Aias
ēïtheon thaleron Simoeision, hon pote mētēr
Idēthen katiousa par’ ochthēisin Simoentos
geinat’, epei rha tokeusin ham’ hespeto mēla idesthai·
sentences.l:
There hit the son of Anthemion Telamonian Ajax,
a young man, flourishing, Simoeisius, whom once his mother,
coming down from Ida beside the banks of the Simois,
bore, when she had followed with her parents to see the flocks;
sentences.i: There Telamonian Ajax hit the son of Anthemion, a flourishing young man, Simoeisius, whom his mother had once borne beside the banks of the Simois, as she was coming down from Ida, when she had gone with her parents to see the flocks;
sentences.n: ἔβαλ’ is ἔβαλε elided, ‘hit’, with Ἀνθεμίωνος υἱόν ‘the son of Anthemion’ as its object and Τελαμώνιος Αἴας as its subject; the adjective ‘Telamonian’ tells this Ajax from Ajax son of Oileus. ἠΐθεον is an unmarried young man, and θαλερόν ‘flourishing’, from the root of θάλλω ‘thrive’, is a second adjective with it. ὅν ποτε μήτηρ … γείνατ’ is ‘whom once his mother bore’ (γείνατο, aorist middle, elided). Ἴδηθεν ‘from Ida’ has the suffix -θεν, κατιοῦσα is the feminine participle of κάτειμι ‘go down’, and ὄχθῃσιν is the epic dative plural -ῃσιν, ‘banks’. ἐπεί ῥα … ἕσπετο is ‘when she had gone with’ (or ‘since’; the Greek allows both): ἕσπετο is an aorist of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, τοκεῦσιν is the dative plural of τοκεύς ‘parent’, ἅμ’ is ‘along with’, and μῆλα is the ‘flocks’ she had gone to see, with ἰδέσθαι (aorist infinitive middle of ὁράω) giving the purpose.

sentences.t: τοὔνεκά μιν κάλεον Σιμοείσιον·
sentences.tr: touneka min kaleon Simoeision·
sentences.l: for that reason they called him Simoeisius;
sentences.i: that is why they called him Simoeisius;
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα run together, ‘for that reason’, and κάλεον is an unaugmented, uncontracted imperfect (Attic ἐκάλουν); μιν is the enclitic ‘him’. The name Σιμοείσιος is built on the river Σιμόεις of 475, so the story explains the name.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ τοκεῦσι
θρέπτρα φίλοις ἀπέδωκε, μινυνθάδιος δέ οἱ αἰὼν
ἔπλεθ’ ὑπ’ Αἴαντος μεγαθύμου δουρὶ δαμέντι.
sentences.tr:
oude tokeusi
threptra philois apedōke, minynthadios de hoi aiōn
epleth’ hyp’ Aiantos megathymou douri damenti.
sentences.l:
and not to his parents
dear, the repayment for rearing did he give back, and short-lived for him his life
was, subdued by great-hearted Ajax with a spear.
sentences.i: and he did not repay his dear parents for his rearing, and his life was short-lived, since he was overcome by great-hearted Ajax with his spear.
sentences.n: ἀπέδωκε is the aorist of ἀποδίδωμι ‘give back, repay’, and θρέπτρα (neuter plural, from τρέφω ‘rear’) is what a son owes his parents for bringing him up; φίλοις ‘dear’ agrees with τοκεῦσι, the dative of the people repaid. μινυνθάδιος ‘short-lived’ goes with αἰών ‘life’ and οἱ ‘for him’, and ἔπλεθ’ is ἔπλετο ‘was’. δαμέντι is the dative aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, agreeing with οἱ, so ‘for him, subdued’; ὑπ’ Αἴαντος marks the agent and δουρί (dative) is the spear, the instrument. Ajax is again μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον γάρ μιν ἰόντα βάλε στῆθος παρὰ μαζὸν
δεξιόν·
sentences.tr:
prōton gar min ionta bale stēthos para mazon
dexion·
sentences.l:
For first, as he came on, he hit him in the chest beside the nipple,
the right one;
sentences.i: For first, as he came on, he hit him in the chest beside the right nipple;
sentences.n: πρῶτον … ἰόντα is ‘first, as he came on’; the Greek does not say whether Simoeisius was in the front line or Ajax struck before others, so ‘first’ stays as it is. γάρ gives the account of his death. βάλε is ‘hit’, with the accusatives στῆθος ‘chest’ and (παρὰ) μαζὸν δεξιόν ‘beside the right nipple’ naming the place struck; μαζός is the breast, here the nipple of a man.

sentences.t:
ἀντικρὺ δὲ δι’ ὤμου χάλκεον ἔγχος
ἦλθεν·
sentences.tr:
antikry de di’ ōmou chalkeon enchos
ēlthen·
sentences.l:
and straight through the shoulder the bronze spear
went;
sentences.i: and the bronze spear went straight through his shoulder;
sentences.n: ἀντικρύ is ‘straight through’, and δι’ ὤμου ‘through the shoulder’ has ὤμου as the genitive of ὦμος. χάλκεον ‘of bronze’ is an adjective agreeing with the neuter ἔγχος ‘spear’, and ἦλθεν ‘went’ is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, used for the spear’s passing through.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι χαμαὶ πέσεν αἴγειρος ὣς
ἥ ῥά τ’ ἐν εἱαμενῇ ἕλεος μεγάλοιο πεφύκει
λείη, ἀτάρ τέ οἱ ὄζοι ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῃ πεφύασι·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ en koniēisi chamai pesen aigeiros hōs
hē rha t’ en heiamenēi heleos megaloio pephykei
leiē, atar te hoi ozoi ep’ akrotatēi pephyasi·
sentences.i: and he fell to the ground in the dust, like a poplar that has grown in the water-meadow of a great marsh, smooth, but with branches growing on its very top;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’; ἐν κονίῃσι χαμαί is ‘in the dust on the ground’, and πέσεν is ἔπεσε, ‘fell’. αἴγειρος ὣς opens the simile, ‘like a poplar’, with ὣς after its noun. ἥ ῥά τ’ … πεφύκει is a relative clause with the epic τε: πεφύκει is a pluperfect of φύω (‘had grown’, with the sense of a state already reached) and the perfect πεφύασι ‘have grown’ stands beside it, both describing how the tree stands; because the tree is standing now, i says ‘has grown’. εἱαμενῇ is low ground by water, a ‘water-meadow’, and ἕλεος μεγάλοιο is the epic genitive of ἕλος ‘marsh’, ‘of a great marsh’. λείη is ‘smooth’, ἀτάρ ‘but’, ὄζοι ‘branches’, and ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῃ ‘on the topmost (part)’; the tree is smooth to the top and then branches.

sentences.t:
τὴν μέν θ’ ἁρματοπηγὸς ἀνὴρ αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ
ἐξέταμ’, ὄφρα ἴτυν κάμψῃ περικαλλέϊ δίφρῳ·
sentences.tr:
tēn men th’ harmatopēgos anēr aithōni sidērōi
exetam’, ophra ityn kampsēi perikalleï diphrōi·
sentences.l:
this a chariot-builder man with fire-bright iron
cuts down, so that he may bend a wheel-rim for a very beautiful chariot;
sentences.i: a chariot-builder cuts it down with fire-bright iron, to bend a wheel-rim for a very beautiful chariot;
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘it’, the poplar, and ἐξέταμ’ is the aorist of ἐκτάμνω ‘cut down’ with its ending elided; as often in similes the aorist states what always happens, so it is rendered in the present. ἁρματοπηγός is ‘chariot-builder’ (ἅρμα ‘chariot’ + πήγνυμι ‘fix’), and αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ ‘fire-bright iron’ is a stock phrase, the dative of the tool. ὄφρα with the subjunctive κάμψῃ gives purpose, ‘so that he may bend’; ἴτυς is the rim of a wheel, bent from one piece of wood. περικαλλέϊ is the dative of περικαλλής ‘very beautiful’, with δίφρῳ ‘chariot’.

sentences.t: ἣ μέν τ’ ἀζομένη κεῖται ποταμοῖο παρ’ ὄχθας.
sentences.tr: hē men t’ azomenē keitai potamoio par’ ochthas.
sentences.l: and it, drying out, lies beside the banks of the river.
sentences.i: and it lies drying out beside the river’s banks.
sentences.n: ἣ is ‘it’, the felled tree, and ἀζομένη is the present participle of ἄζομαι ‘dry up, become parched’, a rare word whose sense is taken from the usual explanation and not otherwise confirmed; κεῖται ‘lies’ is present, and the τε is the epic particle of what is always so. παρ’ ὄχθας is ‘beside the banks’ (accusative plural), with ποταμοῖο the epic genitive of ποταμός ‘river’. The tree that grew by water lies cut beside water.

sentences.t:
τοῖον ἄρ’ Ἀνθεμίδην Σιμοείσιον ἐξενάριξεν
Αἴας διογενής·
sentences.tr:
toion ar’ Anthemidēn Simoeision exenarixen
Aias diogenēs·
sentences.l:
Such a one, then, Anthemion’s-son Simoeisius despoiled
Ajax, Zeus-sprung;
sentences.i: Such, then, was the son of Anthemion, Simoeisius, whom Zeus-born Ajax killed and stripped of his armour;
sentences.n: τοῖον ‘such’ agrees with the accusative Ἀνθεμίδην, a patronymic ‘son of Anthemion’, and takes up the simile: such a one, like the tree, did Ajax strike down. ἐξενάριξεν is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of the arms’ (from ἐνάρα, the spoils of a killed man). διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’ is a stock epithet of heroes; it is used of Ajax here and of Odysseus elsewhere.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ Ἄντιφος αἰολοθώρηξ
Πριαμίδης καθ’ ὅμιλον ἀκόντισεν ὀξέϊ δουρί.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ Antiphos aiolothōrēx
Priamidēs kath’ homilon akontisen oxeï douri.
sentences.l:
and at him Antiphus of the glancing breastplate,
Priam’s-son, through the throng cast with a sharp spear.
sentences.i: and at him Antiphus, son of Priam, with the glancing breastplate, cast his sharp spear through the throng.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the genitive of the target with ἀκόντισεν, ‘at him’, and ‘him’ is Ajax. Ἄντιφος αἰολοθώρηξ is ‘Antiphus of the glancing breastplate’: αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’ + θώρηξ ‘breastplate’, and whether the word means gleaming or flickering is not known. Πριαμίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Priam’, one of Priam’s many sons. καθ’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the throng’; ἀκόντισεν ‘cast a spear’ is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω, from ἄκων ‘javelin’; ὀξέϊ δουρί ‘with a sharp spear’ is the dative of the weapon, printed with a diaeresis.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν ἅμαρθ’, ὃ δὲ Λεῦκον Ὀδυσσέος ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον
βεβλήκει βουβῶνα, νέκυν ἑτέρωσ’ ἐρύοντα·
sentences.tr:
tou men hamarth’, ho de Leukon Odysseos esthlon hetairon
beblēkei boubōna, nekyn heterōs’ eryonta·
sentences.l:
him he missed, but Leucus, Odysseus’ good companion,
he had hit in the groin, as he was dragging the corpse to the other side;
sentences.i: He missed Ajax, but he hit Leucus, Odysseus’ good companion, in the groin as he was dragging the corpse away to the other side;
sentences.n: τοῦ μὲν ἅμαρθ’: ἁμαρτάνω takes the genitive, so ‘missed him’, meaning Ajax; ἅμαρθ’ is an aorist without augment, elided. ὃ δέ is ‘but he’, Antiphus. Λεῦκον … ἑταῖρον is ‘Leucus, the good companion’ of Ὀδυσσέος (the epic genitive of Odysseus), and ἐσθλόν is ‘good’. βεβλήκει is a pluperfect of βάλλω, ‘had hit’, used where English says simply ‘hit’, and βουβῶνα, the groin, is the accusative of the place struck. νέκυν ἑτέρωσ’ ἐρύοντα is ‘dragging the corpse to the other side’ (ἑτέρωσε), the corpse being Simoeisius’; Leucus is named only here.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ, νεκρὸς δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.tr: ēripe d’ amph’ autōi, nekros de hoi ekpese cheiros.
sentences.l: and he crashed down about it, and the corpse fell from his hand.
sentences.i: and he crashed down over it, and the corpse fell from his hand.
sentences.n: ἤριπε is the same verb as at 462 (the tower). ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ is ‘about it’, ἀμφί with the dative, and αὐτῷ is the corpse he had been dragging. ἔκπεσε is the aorist of ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’, with the genitive χειρός ‘from the hand’, and οἱ is ‘his’, a dative of the possessor.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς μάλα θυμὸν ἀποκταμένοιο χολώθη,
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ,
στῆ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰὼν καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ
ἀμφὶ ἓ παπτήνας·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ Odyseus mala thymon apoktamenoio cholōthē,
bē de dia promachōn kekorythmenos aithopi chalkōi,
stē de mal’ engys iōn kai akontise douri phaeinōi
amphi he paptēnas·
sentences.l:
And over him, killed, Odysseus was greatly angered in heart,
and went through the front-fighters, armed with the fire-faced bronze,
and stood, coming very close, and cast with a shining spear,
having looked about him;
sentences.i: Odysseus was greatly angered in his heart at the killing of Leucus; he went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire, took his stand very close, and, after looking about him, cast with his shining spear;
sentences.n: τοῦ … ἀποκταμένοιο is a genitive of cause with χολώθη, ‘angered over him’, and ἀποκταμένοιο is the aorist middle participle of ἀποκτείνω in a passive sense, ‘killed’ (epic -οιο); μάλα θυμόν is an accusative of respect, ‘greatly in heart’, and χολώθη, the aorist passive of χολόω, comes from χόλος ‘anger’. βῆ is ‘went’ (aorist of βαίνω, no augment), and διὰ προμάχων ‘through the front-fighters’ has the genitive plural of πρόμαχος. κεκορυθμένος is the perfect passive participle of κορύσσω ‘arm’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’), and αἴθοπι χαλκῷ ‘fire-faced bronze’ is a stock phrase: αἴθοψ is αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὄψ ‘face’. στῆ is ‘stood’ (aorist of ἵστημι, no augment), μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰών ‘coming very close’; ἀκόντισε ‘cast’ has no object, and δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with a shining spear’. ἀμφὶ ἓ παπτήνας is ‘having looked about him’: ἀμφί is an adverb, ἓ is the reflexive ‘himself’, and παπτήνας is the aorist participle of παπταίνω ‘look around’.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δὲ Τρῶες κεκάδοντο
ἀνδρὸς ἀκοντίσσαντος·
sentences.tr:
hypo de Trōes kekadonto
andros akontissantos·
sentences.l:
and back the Trojans drew away
before the man who had cast;
sentences.i: and the Trojans drew back before the man who had cast his spear;
sentences.n: κεκάδοντο is a reduplicated aorist middle of χάζομαι ‘give way, draw back’, and ὑπό, set apart from its verb (tmesis), is ‘back, away’. ἀνδρὸς ἀκοντίσσαντος is ‘the man having cast’, the aorist participle of ἀκοντίζω with a doubled σ for the metre, in the genitive either as a genitive absolute or as the genitive of the one they gave way before; the sense is the same, ‘before the man who had cast’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ οὐχ ἅλιον βέλος ἧκεν,
ἀλλ’ υἱὸν Πριάμοιο νόθον βάλε Δημοκόωντα
ὅς οἱ Ἀβυδόθεν ἦλθε παρ’ ἵππων ὠκειάων.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ouch halion belos hēken,
all’ huion Priamoio nothon bale Dēmokoōnta
hos hoi Abydothen ēlthe par’ hippōn ōkeiaōn.
sentences.l:
and he did not send a shaft in vain,
but hit Priam’s illegitimate son Democoön,
who to him from Abydos had come from beside swift mares.
sentences.i: He did not send his shaft in vain, but hit Priam’s illegitimate son Democoön, who had come to Priam from Abydos, from beside swift mares.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Odysseus. ἅλιος here is ‘in vain, wasted’ (a different word from ἅλιος ‘of the sea’), βέλος is a ‘shaft’, any missile, and ἧκεν is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’. Πριάμοιο νόθον is ‘the illegitimate son of Priam’, νόθος being ‘born outside marriage’, and Δημοκόωντα the accusative of Democoön. ὅς οἱ Ἀβυδόθεν ἦλθε is ‘who had come to him from Abydos’, οἱ being Priam and -θεν ‘from’; Abydos is on the Hellespont. παρ’ ἵππων ὠκειάων is ‘from beside swift mares’: παρά takes the genitive, and ὠκειάων is the epic feminine genitive plural of ὠκύς, so the horses are mares.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἑτάροιο χολωσάμενος βάλε δουρὶ
κόρσην·
sentences.tr:
ton rh’ Odyseus hetaroio cholōsamenos bale douri
korsēn·
sentences.l:
Him Odysseus, angered for his companion, hit with a spear
on the side of the head;
sentences.i: Odysseus, angered for his companion, hit him with his spear on the side of the head;
sentences.n: τόν ῥ’ is ‘him’, Democoön (τόν is the article as a pronoun, ῥ’ is ῥα). χολωσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of χολόω ‘anger’, with the genitive ἑτάροιο ‘for his companion’ (epic -οιο), and the companion is Leucus. βάλε δουρί is ‘hit with a spear’, and κόρσην is an accusative of the place struck: κόρση is the side of the head by the temple.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἑτέροιο διὰ κροτάφοιο πέρησεν
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη· τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ heteroio dia krotaphoio perēsen
aichmē chalkeiē· ton de skotos osse kalypse,
doupēsen de pesōn, arabēse de teuche’ ep’ autōi.
sentences.l:
and it through the other temple pierced
the bronze point; and darkness covered his two eyes,
and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: and the bronze point pierced through the other temple; and darkness covered his eyes, and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: ἣ is the demonstrative ‘it’, the point named in the next line, and διὰ … πέρησεν is ‘pierced through’, with ἑτέροιο κροτάφοιο ‘the other temple’: the point went in at one side and out at the other. αἰχμὴ χαλκείη is ‘bronze point’ (χαλκείη is the epic form of the adjective). τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε is the line of 461 and 526, with κάλυψε where 461 has κάλυψεν; its English is kept. δούπησεν ‘fell with a thud’ and ἀράβησε ‘clattered’ are sound-words (aorists of δουπέω and ἀραβέω), and the line δούπησεν δὲ πεσών … is the same as Odyssey 24.525, where its English is the same.

sentences.t: χώρησαν δ’ ὑπό τε πρόμαχοι καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: chōrēsan d’ hypo te promachoi kai phaidimos Hektōr·
sentences.l: And back gave way the front-fighters and glorious Hector;
sentences.i: Both the foremost fighters and glorious Hector gave way;
sentences.n: χώρησαν δ’ ὑπό is a tmesis, ὑπό belonging to the verb, aorist of χωρέω ‘give ground’; τε … καὶ is ‘both … and’. πρόμαχοι are ‘front-fighters’, the men who fight before the rest. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is Hector’s stock epithet, usually explained as ‘shining’, and ‘glorious’ is the Odyssey’s rendering of it.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δὲ μέγα ἴαχον, ἐρύσαντο δὲ νεκρούς,
ἴθυσαν δὲ πολὺ προτέρω·
sentences.tr:
Argeioi de mega iachon, erysanto de nekrous,
ithysan de poly proterō·
sentences.l:
and the Argives shouted loudly, and drew off the corpses,
and rushed much farther forward;
sentences.i: while the Argives shouted aloud, dragged off the corpses, and charged far forward;
sentences.n: ἴαχον is an aorist of ἰάχω ‘cry out’, with μέγα as an adverb, ‘loudly’; ἐρύσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω ‘draw, drag’, here ‘dragged off’, to strip the dead; ἴθυσαν is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’. πολὺ προτέρω is ‘much farther forward’, with προτέρω the comparative adverb. Ἀργεῖοι is one of the poet’s three names for the Achaean army.

sentences.t:
νεμέσησε δ’ Ἀπόλλων
Περγάμου ἐκκατιδών, Τρώεσσι δὲ κέκλετ’ ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr:
nemesēse d’ Apollōn
Pergamou ekkatidōn, Trōessi de keklet’ aÿsas·
sentences.l:
and Apollo felt resentment,
looking down from Pergamus, and gave orders to the Trojans, shouting:
sentences.i: and Apollo, looking down from Pergamus, felt resentment, and shouted orders to the Trojans:
sentences.n: νεμέσησε is the aorist of νεμεσάω ‘feel resentment’, with no object: Apollo resents what he sees. ἐκκατιδών is the aorist participle ‘looking down out of’ (ἐκ + κατά + ἰδών in one word), and Περγάμου is the genitive of the place from which; Pergamus is the citadel of Troy. Τρώεσσι is the epic dative plural -εσσι, κέκλετ’ is the reduplicated aorist of κέλομαι ‘order’ (unaugmented, elided), and ἀΰσας is the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’. A speech begins in the next line.

sentences.t:
ὄρνυσθ’ ἱππόδαμοι Τρῶες μηδ’ εἴκετε χάρμης
Ἀργείοις, ἐπεὶ οὔ σφι λίθος χρὼς οὐδὲ σίδηρος
χαλκὸν ἀνασχέσθαι ταμεσίχροα βαλλομένοισιν·
sentences.tr:
ornysth’ hippodamoi Trōes mēd’ eikete charmēs
Argeiois, epei ou sphi lithos chrōs oude sidēros
chalkon anaschesthai tamesichroa ballomenoisin·
sentences.i: “Rouse yourselves, Trojans, tamers of horses, and do not give way to the Argives in the joy of battle, since their skin is not stone, nor iron, to withstand the skin-cutting bronze when they are hit;
sentences.n: ὄρνυσθ’ is the present middle imperative of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, with the ending -ε elided, ‘rouse yourselves’; ἱππόδαμοι ‘horse-taming’ is the Trojans’ stock epithet, in the vocative with Τρῶες. μηδ’ εἴκετε is ‘and do not yield’ (εἴκω), and χάρμης, the genitive of χάρμη ‘joy of battle’, is what they are not to give way from (so i says ‘in the joy of battle’), while Ἀργείοις is the dative ‘to the Argives’. The reason follows: ἐπεὶ οὔ σφι λίθος χρὼς οὐδὲ σίδηρος has σφι as a dative of the possessor (‘to them is not … the skin’) with ‘is’ understood. χρώς is skin, and χαλκὸν ἀνασχέσθαι is ‘to hold out against the bronze’ (aorist infinitive middle of ἀνέχω), with ταμεσίχροα ‘skin-cutting’ (τάμνω ‘cut’ + χρώς) agreeing with χαλκόν; βαλλομένοισιν is a dative plural participle, ‘as they are hit’, with the epic ending -οισιν, agreeing with σφι.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰν οὐδ’ Ἀχιλεὺς Θέτιδος πάϊς ἠϋκόμοιο
μάρναται, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶ χόλον θυμαλγέα πέσσει.
sentences.tr:
ou man oud’ Achileus Thetidos païs ēÿkomoio
marnatai, all’ epi nēusi cholon thymalgea pessei.
sentences.l:
truly not even Achilles, son of fine-haired Thetis,
is fighting, but at the ships heart-paining anger he cooks.”
sentences.i: Truly, not even Achilles, son of fine-haired Thetis, is fighting; at the ships he broods over an anger that pains his heart.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὰν οὐδ’ is ‘truly not even’ (μάν ‘truly’). Θέτιδος πάϊς ἠϋκόμοιο is ‘son of fine-haired Thetis’: πάϊς is παῖς, and ἠΰκομος ‘fine-haired’ is Thetis’s stock epithet. μάρναται is the present of μάρναμαι ‘fight’, and ἐπὶ νηυσί ‘at the ships’ has the epic dative plural of ναῦς. χόλον θυμαλγέα πέσσει: πέσσω is ‘cook, digest’, and to ‘cook’ one’s anger is to brood over it; θυμαλγέα ‘heart-paining’ (θυμός ‘heart’ + ἄλγος ‘pain’) agrees with χόλον. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’ ἀπὸ πτόλιος δεινὸς θεός·
sentences.tr: hōs phat’ apo ptolios deinos theos·
sentences.l: So spoke from the city the dread god;
sentences.i: So the dread god spoke from the city;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ is the formula that closes a speech, ‘so he spoke’ (φάτ’ is ἔφατο, unaugmented, elided). ἀπὸ πτόλιος is ‘from the city’, πτόλις being the older form of πόλις, and δεινὸς θεός ‘the dread god’ is Apollo, with δεινός ‘dread’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
ὦρσε Διὸς θυγάτηρ κυδίστη Τριτογένεια
ἐρχομένη καθ’ ὅμιλον, ὅθι μεθιέντας ἴδοιτο.
sentences.tr:
autar Achaious
ōrse Dios thygatēr kydistē Tritogeneia
erchomenē kath’ homilon, hothi methientas idoito.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
roused the daughter of Zeus, most glorious Tritogeneia,
going through the throng, wherever she might see them slackening.
sentences.i: but the daughter of Zeus, most glorious Tritogeneia, roused the Achaeans as she went through the throng, wherever she saw them slackening.
sentences.n: ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, the verb of Apollo’s ὄρνυσθ’, so each side is roused by a god. Διὸς θυγάτηρ ‘the daughter of Zeus’ is Athena, who is not named (the phrase Διὸς θυγάτηρ, κυδίστη Τριτογένεια also stands at Odyssey 3.378, with the same English); κυδίστη ‘most glorious’ is the superlative of the κῦδος family, and Τριτογένεια is a title of Athena whose meaning is not known (the guesses are ‘born at the river or lake Triton’, ‘head’ and ‘third-born’). ἐρχομένη is ‘going’, καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’, and μεθιέντας is the participle of μεθίημι ‘let go, slacken’; ὅθι … ἴδοιτο is an indefinite clause, ‘wherever she should see’, with the aorist optative middle of ὁράω.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Ἀμαρυγκείδην Διώρεα μοῖρα πέδησε·
sentences.tr: enth’ Amarynkeidēn Diōrea moira pedēse·
sentences.l: There Amarynceus’-son Diores his portion bound;
sentences.i: There fate bound Diores, the son of Amarynceus;
sentences.n: Ἀμαρυγκείδην is a patronymic accusative, ‘son of Amarynceus’, and Διώρεα is the accusative of Διώρης; he is the Epean leader of line 537. μοῖρα is ‘portion’, one’s allotted share, and so ‘fate’; πέδησε is the aorist of πεδάω ‘bind, fetter’, so fate bound him as with a fetter, and the next lines show how. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
χερμαδίῳ γὰρ βλῆτο παρὰ σφυρὸν ὀκριόεντι
κνήμην δεξιτερήν·
sentences.tr:
chermadiōi gar blēto para sphyron okrioenti
knēmēn dexiterēn·
sentences.l:
for with a jagged rock he was hit beside the ankle,
on the right shin;
sentences.i: for he was hit with a jagged rock beside the ankle, on the right shin;
sentences.n: χερμαδίῳ ὀκριόεντι is ‘with a jagged rock’, a dative of the instrument (χερμάδιον, a stone to throw; ὀκριόεις ‘jagged’, from ὄκρις ‘point’). βλῆτο is the aorist middle of βάλλω (ἔβλητο, without augment), with passive sense, ‘was hit’. παρὰ σφυρόν is ‘beside the ankle’, and κνήμην δεξιτερήν ‘the right shin’ is an accusative of the part struck; δεξιτερός is a longer form of δεξιός.

sentences.t:
βάλε δὲ Θρῃκῶν ἀγὸς ἀνδρῶν
Πείρως Ἰμβρασίδης ὃς ἄρ’ Αἰνόθεν εἰληλούθει.
sentences.tr:
bale de Thrēikōn agos andrōn
Peirōs Imbrasidēs hos ar’ Ainothen eilēlouthei.
sentences.l:
and hit him the leader of Thracian men,
Peirous, Imbrasus’-son, who had come from Aenus.
sentences.i: It was Peirous, son of Imbrasus, leader of the Thracian men, who hit him; he had come from Aenus.
sentences.n: βάλε δέ is ‘and hit’, the subject coming only in the next line, Πείρως ‘Peirous’ (Πείροος at 525 is the same man). Θρῃκῶν ἀγὸς ἀνδρῶν is ‘leader of the Thracian men’ (ἀγός ‘leader’, from ἄγω), and Ἰμβρασίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Imbrasus’. ὃς ἄρ’ Αἰνόθεν εἰληλούθει is ‘who had come from Aenus’, a town in Thrace: -θεν is ‘from’, and εἰληλούθει is the pluperfect of ἔρχομαι. The Thracians and Peirous are in the Trojan Catalogue at 2.844.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρω δὲ τένοντε καὶ ὀστέα λᾶας ἀναιδὴς
ἄχρις ἀπηλοίησεν·
sentences.tr:
amphoterō de tenonte kai ostea laas anaidēs
achris apēloiēsen·
sentences.l:
and both tendons and the bones the shameless stone
utterly crushed;
sentences.i: and the ruthless stone crushed both tendons and the bones utterly;
sentences.n: ἀμφοτέρω δὲ τένοντε καὶ ὀστέα is ‘both tendons and the bones’, with τένοντε a dual. λᾶας ἀναιδής is ‘the shameless stone’: ἀναιδής ‘shameless’ is used of a stone that spares nothing, and i gives ‘ruthless’; the phrase is the same as the Odyssey’s for the stone of Sisyphus. ἄχρις is ‘utterly’, and ἀπηλοίησεν is the aorist of ἀπαλοιάω ‘crush’, a rare verb whose sense is taken from the usual explanation.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος ἐν κονίῃσι
κάππεσεν ἄμφω χεῖρε φίλοις ἑτάροισι πετάσσας
θυμὸν ἀποπνείων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hyptios en koniēisi
kappesen amphō cheire philois hetaroisi petassas
thymon apopneiōn·
sentences.i: and he fell down on his back in the dust, spreading out both hands to his dear companions, breathing out his life;
sentences.n: ὕπτιος is ‘on his back’. κάππεσεν is κατέπεσεν, ‘fell down’, with the α of κατά cut short and its τ made into π before the π of πεσ-. ἄμφω χεῖρε is ‘both hands’ (dual), φίλοις ἑτάροισι ‘to his dear companions’ (dative), and πετάσσας is the aorist participle of πετάννυμι ‘spread out’. θυμὸν ἀποπνείων is ‘breathing out his life’ (a present participle), θυμός being the life again, as at 470.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐπέδραμεν ὅς ῥ’ ἔβαλέν περ
Πείροος, οὖτα δὲ δουρὶ παρ’ ὀμφαλόν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epedramen hos rh’ ebalen per
Peiroos, outa de douri par’ omphalon·
sentences.l:
and he ran up, he who had hit him indeed,
Peirous, and wounded him with a spear beside the navel;
sentences.i: and Peirous, the very man who had hit him, ran up and stabbed him with his spear beside the navel;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἐπέδραμεν is ‘and he ran up’ (aorist of ἐπιτρέχω); ὅς ῥ’ ἔβαλέν περ Πείροος is ‘who had indeed hit (him), Peirous’, where περ intensifies the relative (‘the very one who’), the ν of ἔβαλέν is the movable ν, and the aorist looks back to 519, ‘had hit’. Πείροος is the longer form of the name Πείρως at 520. οὖτα is an aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’, the verb of οὔτησε at 469, here with δουρί ‘with a spear’ and παρ’ ὀμφαλόν ‘beside the navel’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα πᾶσαι
χύντο χαμαὶ χολάδες, τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε.
sentences.tr:
ek d’ ara pasai
chynto chamai cholades, ton de skotos osse kalypse.
sentences.l:
and out then all his bowels
poured to the ground, and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: and all his bowels poured out upon the ground, and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: ἐκ … χύντο is a tmesis, ‘poured out’: χύντο is the aorist middle of χέω ‘pour’, and χαμαί is ‘to the ground’. πᾶσαι ‘all’ agrees with χολάδες, feminine plural, ‘bowels’; ἄρα is ‘then’. τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε is the line of 461 and 503, ‘and darkness covered his two eyes’, so the same formula closes three deaths in this part.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ Θόας Αἰτωλὸς ἀπεσσύμενον βάλε δουρὶ
στέρνον ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο, πάγη δ’ ἐν πνεύμονι χαλκός·
sentences.tr:
ton de Thoas Aitōlos apessymenon bale douri
sternon hyper mazoio, pagē d’ en pneumoni chalkos·
sentences.l:
And him, as he rushed away, Thoas the Aetolian hit with a spear
in the breast above the nipple, and in the lung was fixed the bronze;
sentences.i: Thoas the Aetolian hit him with a spear as he rushed away, in the breast above the nipple, and the bronze stuck fast in his lung;
sentences.n: τὸν is Peirous. ἀπεσσύμενον is the perfect middle participle of ἀποσεύομαι ‘dart off’ (ἔσσυμαι, with a doubled σ), present in sense, ‘rushing away’, so Peirous is rushing away from his kill. Θόας Αἰτωλός is ‘Thoas the Aetolian’, the subject, and βάλε δουρί is ‘hit with a spear’; στέρνον ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο is ‘in the breast above the nipple’, στέρνον being the breast where στῆθος is the chest. πάγη is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, without augment, ‘was fixed’, and ἐν πνεύμονι ‘in the lung’; χαλκός ‘bronze’ stands for the spear-head. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δέ οἱ ἦλθε Θόας, ἐκ δ’ ὄβριμον ἔγχος
ἐσπάσατο στέρνοιο, ἐρύσσατο δὲ ξίφος ὀξύ,
τῷ ὅ γε γαστέρα τύψε μέσην, ἐκ δ’ αἴνυτο θυμόν.
sentences.tr:
anchimolon de hoi ēlthe Thoas, ek d’ obrimon enchos
espasato sternoio, eryssato de xiphos oxy,
tōi ho ge gastera typse mesēn, ek d’ ainyto thymon.
sentences.l:
And close by him came Thoas, and out the mighty spear
he pulled from the breast, and drew his sharp sword,
with it he struck him in the middle of the belly, and took away his life.
sentences.i: Thoas came close by him, and pulled his mighty spear out of the breast, and drew his sharp sword, and with it struck him in the middle of the belly and took away his life.
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is ‘close by’ (adverb), and οἱ is ‘to him’, Peirous; the half-line ἀγχίμολον δέ οἱ ἦλθε also stands at Odyssey 15.95, and its English is kept. ἐκ δ’ … ἐσπάσατο is a tmesis, ‘pulled out’ (aorist middle of σπάω), with στέρνοιο, the genitive of separation, ‘from the breast’, and ὄβριμον ‘mighty’ the stock epithet of the spear. ἐρύσσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, and ξίφος ὀξύ is ‘sharp sword’. τῷ ὅ γε is ‘with it he’, τῷ being the sword and ὅ γε Thoas; γαστέρα … μέσην is ‘the belly in the middle’, an accusative of the place struck, and τύψε is the aorist of τύπτω ‘strike’. ἐκ δ’ αἴνυτο θυμόν is ‘and took away his life’ (tmesis; αἴνυτο, from αἴνυμαι ‘take’, has no augment).

sentences.t: τεύχεα δ’ οὐκ ἀπέδυσε·
sentences.tr: teuchea d’ ouk apedyse·
sentences.l: and the armour he did not strip off;
sentences.i: But he did not strip off the armour;
sentences.n: τεύχεα is the ‘armour’ (neuter plural) of Peirous, and ἀπέδυσε is the active aorist of ἀποδύω, which as a transitive verb means ‘strip off’. The subject is Thoas, and the next lines say why he could not.

sentences.t:
περίστησαν γὰρ ἑταῖροι
Θρήϊκες ἀκρόκομοι δολίχ’ ἔγχεα χερσὶν ἔχοντες,
οἵ ἑ μέγαν περ ἐόντα καὶ ἴφθιμον καὶ ἀγαυὸν
ὦσαν ἀπὸ σφείων·
sentences.tr:
peristēsan gar hetairoi
Thrēïkes akrokomoi dolich’ enchea chersin echontes,
hoi he megan per eonta kai iphthimon kai agauon
ōsan apo spheiōn·
sentences.i: for Peirous’ companions stood around, topknotted Thracians with long spears in their hands, and pushed him away from them, great though he was, and mighty and noble;
sentences.n: περίστησαν γάρ is ‘for they stood around’ (aorist of περιΐστημι, here intransitive); ἑταῖροι Θρήϊκες is ‘companions, Thracians’, the men of Peirous. ἀκρόκομοι ‘topknotted’ is ἄκρος ‘top’ + κόμη ‘hair’, and is usually taken to mean hair worn in a knot on the crown, but the exact fashion is not known. δολίχ’ ἔγχεα is ‘long spears’, and χερσὶν ἔχοντες ‘holding in their hands’. οἵ is the relative ‘who’ and ἑ ‘him’, Thoas; μέγαν περ ἐόντα καὶ ἴφθιμον καὶ ἀγαυόν is ‘great though he was, and mighty, and noble’, a concessive περ with the participle ἐόντα and three accusative adjectives. ὦσαν ἀπὸ σφείων is ‘pushed him away from themselves’ (ὦσαν aorist of ὠθέω, σφείων the epic genitive plural ‘them’).

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ χασσάμενος πελεμίχθη.
sentences.tr: ho de chassamenos pelemichthē.
sentences.l: and he, having given ground, was shaken.
sentences.i: and he gave ground, reeling.
sentences.n: ὃ δὲ is Thoas. χασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of χάζομαι ‘give ground’ (the verb of κεκάδοντο at 497), and πελεμίχθη is the aorist passive of πελεμίζω ‘shake, make reel’, without augment: struck back by the spears, he reeled.

sentences.t:
ὣς τώ γ’ ἐν κονίῃσι παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι τετάσθην,
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν Θρῃκῶν, ὃ δ’ Ἐπειῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
ἡγεμόνες·
sentences.tr:
hōs tō g’ en koniēisi par’ allēloisi tetasthēn,
ētoi ho men Thrēikōn, ho d’ Epeiōn chalkochitōnōn
hēgemones·
sentences.i: So the two of them lay stretched out in the dust beside one another, the one a leader of the Thracians, the other of the bronze-shirted Epeans;
sentences.n: ὣς τώ γ’ is ‘so those two’: τώ is the dual of the article used as a pronoun, here Diores and Peirous. τετάσθην is the dual pluperfect passive of τείνω ‘stretch’, without augment, ‘had been stretched out’, that is, lay. παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι is ‘beside one another’. ἤτοι ὃ μέν … ὃ δ’ is ‘the one … the other’, and Θρῃκῶν and Ἐπειῶν χαλκοχιτώνων are genitives depending on ἡγεμόνες ‘leaders’, which stands in apposition to τώ. The Epeans are the men of Elis, and χαλκοχιτών ‘bronze-shirted’ is a stock epithet, here of the Epeans.

sentences.t: πολλοὶ δὲ περὶ κτείνοντο καὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr: polloi de peri kteinonto kai alloi.
sentences.l: and many others besides were being killed around.
sentences.i: and many others were being killed around them.
sentences.n: πολλοὶ … καὶ ἄλλοι is ‘many others as well’, περί an adverb ‘around’, and κτείνοντο the imperfect passive of κτείνω ‘kill’, ‘were being killed’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν οὐκέτι ἔργον ἀνὴρ ὀνόσαιτο μετελθών,
ὅς τις ἔτ’ ἄβλητος καὶ ἀνούτατος ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
δινεύοι κατὰ μέσσον, ἄγοι δέ ἑ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
χειρὸς ἑλοῦσ’, αὐτὰρ βελέων ἀπερύκοι ἐρωήν·
sentences.tr:
entha ken ouketi ergon anēr onosaito metelthōn,
hos tis et’ ablētos kai anoutatos oxeï chalkōi
dineuoi kata messon, agoi de he Pallas Athēnē
cheiros helous’, autar beleōn aperykoi erōēn·
sentences.l:
There no longer would a man make light of the work, going among it,
whoever, still unhit and unwounded by sharp bronze,
might wheel about in the middle, and Pallas Athena lead him
taking him by the hand, and keep off the rush of the shafts;
sentences.i: There a man going among that work would no longer make light of it, whoever, still unhit and unwounded by sharp bronze, might wheel about in the midst, with Pallas Athena leading him by the hand and keeping off the force of the shafts;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the poet turns to an imagined onlooker. κεν with the optative ὀνόσαιτο (aorist of ὄνομαι ‘make light of, scorn’, the sense the Odyssey’s ὄνοσαι and ὀνόσσεσθαι carry) is a potential, ‘would find fault’; ἔργον is ‘the work’ of war, and μετελθών is the aorist participle ‘going among it’. The man is then described by a relative clause with optatives, ὅς τις … δινεύοι … ἄγοι … ἀπερύκοι, ‘whoever should wheel … and lead … and keep off’. ἄβλητος ‘unhit’ and ἀνούτατος ‘unwounded’ are ἀ- + βάλλω and ἀ- + οὐτάω, and ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘sharp bronze’ is the dative of the agent or weapon; δινεύοι is ‘wheel about’, and κατὰ μέσσον ‘in the middle’ (κατά with the accusative, ‘throughout’). ἑ is ‘him’, χειρὸς ἑλοῦσ’ is ‘taking him by the hand’ (the aorist participle of αἱρέω, elided, with the genitive of the part held), and ἐρωήν is the ‘rush’ or force of the shafts, with βελέων ‘of shafts’ depending on it.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ γὰρ Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ἤματι κείνῳ
πρηνέες ἐν κονίῃσι παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι τέταντο.
sentences.tr:
polloi gar Trōōn kai Achaiōn ēmati keinōi
prēnees en koniēisi par’ allēloisi tetanto.
sentences.l:
for many of the Trojans and Achaeans on that day
headlong in the dust beside one another had been stretched out.
sentences.i: For on that day many of the Trojans and Achaeans lay stretched out face down in the dust beside one another.
sentences.n: γάρ ties this line to the one before: the fighting was so thick that many lay dead. Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν is the genitive of the whole, ‘of Trojans and Achaeans’, and ἤματι κείνῳ is ‘on that day’ (κείνῳ is ἐκείνῳ). πρηνέες is ‘headlong, face down’, the nominative plural of πρηνής, and τέταντο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω, ‘had been stretched out’, the verb of τετάσθην at 536, so the line echoes the two leaders lying side by side. The part ends here.
